summary: Procore Technologies acquired construction AI startup Datagrid in January 2026 to embed agentic AI that can automate submittals, RFIs and other document-heavy construction workflows.

body_html:
This news summary was compiled by the PCI editorial team from publicly reported sources. Details are as reported at the time of writing; see the linked source below for the full report.

Procore brings Datagrid's agentic AI in-house

According to Procore Technologies, the construction-management software company completed its acquisition of Datagrid, a vertical artificial-intelligence startup, in January 2026. Procore said the financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

According to Procore and reporting by Engineering News-Record and Construction Dive, Datagrid is an AI platform that connects drawings, specifications and schedules from multiple construction and financial-management systems into a single workspace. Procore described the technology as agentic AI that goes beyond chatbots to execute multi-step tasks such as autonomously managing submittal reviews and drafting requests for information (RFIs) across platforms.

According to Procore, the acquisition is intended to accelerate its AI strategy and strengthen data connectivity for customers by breaking down data silos and automating document-heavy workflows. According to Procore, Datagrid co-founder and chief executive Thiago Da Costa is joining Procore to help lead its AI and data strategy.

According to Construction Dive, the deal reflects a broader wave of consolidation in construction technology as established platforms move to add generative and agentic AI capabilities. Procore has said it plans to embed Datagrid's capabilities natively within its platform, with broader availability expected to follow an initial beta period.

Search results did not disclose a purchase price, the size of Datagrid's team, or detailed integration timelines beyond Procore's statements, and these points should be confirmed against the primary source before publication.

NISTA reports on the UK's biggest projects

The National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA) has published its Major Projects Annual Report 2025-26, providing a snapshot of the performance of the government's most significant programmes between April 2025 and March 2026. According to GOV.UK, NISTA was formed on 1 April 2025 through the merger of the Infrastructure and Projects Authority (IPA) and the National Infrastructure Commission (NIC).

Delivery confidence ratings

The report covers the Government Major Projects Portfolio (GMPP), which the publication describes as the public sector's most complex, innovative and high-value programmes across transport, defence, health, digital transformation and energy. GOV.UK states the 2025-26 portfolio comprised 189 projects with a combined whole-life cost of around £924.2bn and an expected £603.6bn of monetised benefits over the lifetime of the projects.

On delivery confidence, the report indicates that most projects were rated green or amber. GOV.UK reports 29 projects (15%) rated green and 109 (58%) amber, with 34 (18%) rated red and a further 17 (9%) exempt from a delivery confidence assessment. NISTA frames green and amber ratings as projects that are on track or remain deliverable with effective management.

Support for struggling projects

The report says red-rated projects are receiving more intensive support intended to resolve issues before they escalate. Commentators reporting on the publication have noted that many major infrastructure and construction projects still require intervention to stay on track. Coverage of the strategy reports a headline commitment of around £725bn of infrastructure investment over the next decade. Shortly afterwards, on 17 July 2025, NISTA launched its first interactive 10-year Infrastructure Pipeline digital portal. Reports on the launch state the portal initially featured roughly 775 schemes and set out about £530bn of funding, with interactive and downloadable detail on anticipated spend, current project status, expected completion dates and the pipeline methodology.

According to those reports, the pipeline includes capital and maintenance costs for economic infrastructure projects of £25m or more and social infrastructure projects of £15m or more, with further updates expected as departmental business planning progresses.

title: PMI's Pulse of the Profession 2026 puts the spotlight on complex projects

summary: The Project Management Institute's Pulse of the Profession 2026 report focuses on rising project complexity, arguing that traditional best practices alone are no longer enough and that systems thinking is central to success.

body_html:

Navigating complexity, not just tasks

The Project Management Institute (PMI) has released its annual Pulse of the Profession 2026 report, subtitled “Driving Success in Complex Projects: From Navigating Tasks to Navigating Systems.” PMI-related channels indicate the report was released around May 2026.

Key findings reported by PMI

According to PMI, the research finds that 81% of project professionals say projects have become more complex in recent years, that 97% managed at least one complex project in the past year, and that more than half of all projects now qualify as complex. PMI reports that teams which manage complexity effectively are around five times more likely to succeed, and that nearly one-third (31%) of complex projects fail to achieve their intended benefits — more than twice the rate reported for projects overall.

AI and the skills gap

PMI's summary also highlights artificial intelligence as both a driver of complexity and a capability gap. The organisation reports that project professionals expect the share of projects they manage using AI to rise from around 23% to 37% over the next three years, while only about one in five say they have extensive or good practical experience with AI tools.

PMI frames systems thinking — understanding the interconnected people, technology and external forces shaping projects — as central to delivering value in complex environments. Editors should confirm the specific statistics and release date against the PMI source before publishing.

According to APM, the survey was carried out by the research company YouGov, drawing on more than 3,800 project professionals, with fieldwork conducted in late 2024. APM reports that a majority of respondents rated their economic prospects for the year ahead as excellent or good and that job satisfaction across the profession remained high.

According to APM's announcement, from 21 January 2026 the organisation is transitioning from fixed assessment cycles to an ongoing results-release process.

What changes for applicants

APM reports that the final fixed submission deadline under the current system is 20 January 2026, with those results released on 25 February 2026. Under the new approach, APM says applicants will be able to submit their applications when they are ready, with results released approximately 35 working days later — a model APM describes as similar to that used for its qualifications.

According to APM, the change is intended to offer greater flexibility and improve the overall applicant experience by removing the need to wait for a specific submission window. The association also notes that structured deadlines have helped some individuals and cohorts set goals, and it encourages applicants to set personalised target dates aligned with their own preparation.

The California High-Speed Rail Authority has approved a team to build the track and systems for the state's high-speed rail line, a step the Authority frames as delivering the nation's first true high-speed rail. According to the Authority and multiple trade reports, the contract is valued at up to $3.5 billion.

Scope of the work

The award reportedly went to a joint venture of Kiewit, Stacy Witbeck and Herzog (identified in board materials as KSWH JV). The consortium is to install track, the overhead contact system, and train control and communications equipment to transform the 119-mile guideway completed in the Central Valley into an electrified high-speed system capable of speeds up to 220 mph.

Construction advances on India's first bullet train

The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR) project, India's first high-speed rail corridor, continues to advance, according to the Government of India's Press Information Bureau and other reports. The 508 km corridor links Maharashtra and Gujarat and is being built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.

Progress reported

Reports in 2026 describe overall progress at roughly 55–60%, with hundreds of kilometres of pier and viaduct work completed and installation of overhead electrification masts underway along the corridor. The line is being delivered by the National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL).

Tunnelling milestone under the Panama Canal

Crews building Panama Metro Line 3 celebrated a tunnelling breakthrough on the section running beneath the Panama Canal, according to Railway News and other coverage. Reports date the breakthrough at the Balboa shaft to early February 2026, after crews advanced approximately 3 km of the tunnel, with a further section remaining before the final breakthrough at Albrook.

A first for the region

Line 3 is described as the first monorail system in the Americas, using a straddle-type monorail and Japanese technology. The line is reported to run about 24.5 km with 14 stations, connecting Albrook station on Line 1 to the Arraiján area in Panamá Oeste, west of the canal, with a deep underground crossing beneath the waterway reported to reach depths of up to around 64 metres.

  • Milestone: tunnelling breakthrough beneath the Panama Canal (reported February 2026).
  • Line: reported at about 24.5 km with 14 stations.
  • Technology: straddle-type monorail, described as the first in the Americas.

Reports differ on the project's overall cost and opening date, so those figures are omitted here pending verification. The underground crossing of the canal is one of the most technically demanding elements of the scheme, which is intended to improve connections between Panama City and communities to the west.

Editors should confirm the breakthrough date, line length, station count, cost and opening schedule against official Metro de Panamá sources before publishing.

One of the largest data center commitments to date

Meta has committed more than $50 billion to its data center project in Richland Parish, in rural northeast Louisiana, according to Louisiana Economic Development and multiple news reports in July 2026. The campus is home to Hyperion, described as the company's largest AI training cluster.

Scale and power

Reports describe the campus expanding to nearly 10 million square feet and up to 5 gigawatts of IT capacity, making it one of the largest data centers ever built and the largest in Meta's global fleet. Tunnel boring machines break through at Belfiore

Florence's high-speed rail bypass has reached a major milestone, with two tunnel boring machines breaking through into the future Firenze Belfiore station cavern, according to The Florentine. The achievement, reported in early July 2026, completes the southern section of excavation and brings the tunnelling work to around 60% complete.

Purpose of the bypass

The project is designed to separate high-speed rail traffic from regional and freight services, easing congestion across Florence's busy rail network and cutting journey times for long-distance trains. Coverage reports the two machines each travelled roughly three kilometres from the Campo di Marte site before reaching the station cavern; the scheme is reported to be a €2.7 billion investment.

  • Milestone: two TBMs broke through into the future Belfiore station (reported July 2026).
  • Progress: tunnelling reported at around 60% complete.
  • Reported value: €2.7 billion.

Reports indicate excavation of the remaining northern section is expected to resume around the turn of 2026–27, with overall construction scheduled for completion by around the end of 2029 and passenger services expected from 2030. The milestone was marked by a ceremony attended by national and regional officials.

title: PMI Launches Updated PMP Exam for July 2026
seo_title: PMI Launches Updated PMP Exam in July 2026
summary: The Project Management Institute has introduced an updated Project Management Professional (PMP) exam for new candidates from July 2026, built on a revised Exam Content Outline with rebalanced domains and new question formats.
meta_description: PMI has introduced an updated PMP exam for new candidates from July 2026, with a revised Exam Content Outline and new question types.
body_html:
This news summary was compiled by the PCI editorial team from publicly reported sources. Details are as reported at the time of writing; see the linked source below for the full report.

PMI moves new PMP candidates to an updated exam

The Project Management Institute (PMI) has introduced an updated version of its Project Management Professional (PMP) examination, which PMI says takes effect for new candidates in July 2026. According to reporting on the change, the previous exam remained available up to early July 2026, after which only the revised version is offered.

What PMI says is changing

PMI states the update is built on a revised Exam Content Outline. Coverage of the change describes a rebalancing of the three exam domains, with the Business Environment domain carrying more weight than before and the People and Process domains adjusted accordingly. PMI links the revision to a greater emphasis on connecting project work to business outcomes, working across complex stakeholder environments, and exercising judgement in situations increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence and sustainability considerations.

Other reported changes include an updated eligibility window, under which qualifying project experience is counted over a longer look-back period, and new, more interactive question formats such as scenario sets and decision-focused items. PMI also positions the exam alongside its evolving standards, including the eighth edition of the PMBOK Guide.

Why it matters

The PMP is one of the most widely held project-management credentials internationally, so changes to its exam affect training providers, employers and candidates. Prospective candidates and course providers should confirm current eligibility rules, fees and exam formats directly with PMI, as details reported by third parties can lag official updates.

PCI notes this is a developing story; the domain weightings and dates summarised here should be confirmed against PMI's official certification pages before being relied upon.

Source: Project Management Institute.

PMI projects a major shortfall in project professionals

Construction in focus

PMI frames the findings as a call for investment in training, upskilling and structured career development to build the project-management capacity that major programmes — including infrastructure and net-zero projects — will require. The analysis emphasises the value employers place on recognised credentials and continuing professional development.

APM to trial a new ChPP assessment

APM says the pilot focuses on the assessment construct only, with the chartered standard, pathways and underlying competences remaining unchanged. RICS updates its assessment framework with a new resit policy

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) has updated its assessment framework with a new policy on the number of attempts candidates may make. According to RICS, from 1 January 2026 candidates may make up to five attempts to pass a RICS assessment.

How the cap works

Reporting on the change indicates that candidates pursuing Chartered (MRICS) or Associate (AssocRICS) membership will have up to four attempts per membership grade, with the option to apply for a fifth and final attempt after completing a further period of experience. RICS says attempts made before 1 January 2026 do not count towards the total, and that a referral after that date — including where a candidate changes their sector pathway — is treated as an attempt.

Appeals

According to the reporting, where a candidate successfully appeals a referral, or a complaint is upheld and an interview result is set aside, that outcome does not count as an attempt under the new policy.

RICS assessments, including the Assessment of Professional Competence (APC), are competency-based and are relevant to quantity surveying and construction professionals working in project controls. PCI advises candidates to confirm the current rules in the latest RICS candidate guidance, as assessment policies are periodically amended.

Source: Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors.

title: New Competence Framework for Built-Environment PMs
seo_title: New Competence Framework for Built-Environment PMs

meta_description: A new competence framework for built-environment project managers, linked to the Building Safety Act, launched in September 2025.
body_html:
This news summary was compiled by the PCI editorial team from publicly reported sources. Details are as reported at the time of writing; see the linked source below for the full report.

New competence framework for project managers in the built environment

A new competence framework for people managing projects in the built environment has been launched, intended to help project managers meet obligations under the Building Safety Act in England. The framework has been reported by the Chartered Institute of Building (CIOB) and the Association for Project Management (APM).

Origins and governance

According to the reporting, the framework was developed through work that followed the Grenfell Tower tragedy, as part of a wider programme that identified a set of specialisms across construction and the built environment. A dedicated working group focused on project managers was chaired by Gill Hancock of APM, working with CIOB and the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS).

Transition timeline

Sources state that from September 2025 until 2027, project managers in the built environment can demonstrate competence either by achieving certification against the new framework, or by holding chartered status with APM, CIOB or RICS together with relevant built-environment experience. From September 2027, competence is reported to be demonstrable only through assessment against the new framework.

PCI reports these arrangements from CIOB and APM materials and related coverage. Because the framework is tied to regulatory obligations, professionals should confirm the current requirements and transition dates with CIOB, APM or RICS before relying on them.

Source: Chartered Institute of Building.

The ECITB supports employers through mechanisms including training grants, new-entrant programmes, a skills charter and regional skills funding, financed via an industrial training levy. The board frames its strategy around meeting the volume of workers required as project activity increases across the sector.
